tagline: Free, private, offline e-book reader for iOS with on-device read-aloud
summary: Covers the whole 20-point MVP spec in about 5.2k lines of Swift. It parses 8 formats with its own parsers, including MOBI/AZW3 HUFF/CDIC decompression. It reads aloud with continuous playback, background audio, lock-screen controls and sentence highlighting, offers optional neural voices that run on the device, and falls back to Vision OCR for scanned PDFs. Compared with established readers, the main gaps are your own highlights and notes, dictionary lookup, a sleep timer and cross-device sync.

items: EPUB, PDF, TXT, HTML, DOCX, FB2, MOBI and AZW3, using in-house ZIP, XML and MOBI parsers
Import from Files and the Share Sheet, download from a link, document scan and photo import
DRM detection and rejection
List of free legal book sources
Grid and list views with cover, format badge and progress
Sort by recently read, recently added, title, author or progress
Search, collections and delete
Book info sheet with metadata and file size
TextKit reader with position tracking
Light, sepia and dark themes, plus font family, size, line spacing and margins
Table of contents, chapter navigation and bookmarks
Full-text search inside a book
Original-page view for PDFs, through PDFKit
AVSpeechSynthesizer voices, plus optional Kokoro and Piper neural voices downloaded on demand
Play, pause, skip, speed control and continuous playback across chapters
Background audio and lock-screen controls
Spoken sentence highlighted in sync with the reading position
Mini-player in the library
Uses the PDF text layer when there is one, and Vision OCR otherwise
Lazy per-chapter content store cached in Application Support

risks: There's one commit, so changes so far aren't recorded separately
The sherpa-onnx and onnxruntime frameworks (over 100 MB) aren't in git. A clean build depends on scripts/fetch-frameworks.sh still working
The test target is thin. The parsers (MOBI HUFF/CDIC, EPUB TOC) deserve fixture-based tests
App Store review: needs a privacy manifest, and a check on how downloaded neural-voice models are described
